Is Elon Musk coming for your game development job? I would like to address a few key points regarding the viability of using generative AI in game development, both now and in the future. AI generative games will likely produce more games but lower the overall quality of content, rather than improve it. The economic pressures in the gaming industry may prompt some studios to utilize generative AI to create mediocre or sloppy games without much care or polish. Look at YouTube and all the generative AI videos—most of them are pretty much garbage. The tools currently available are still in their early stages and require significant human effort to meet the quality standards needed for games. In the future, AI tools are expected to continue improving and could potentially enhance content creation with minimal human input; however, this is still a long way off. I strongly support the use of AI in game development, but it won't replace game developers when it comes to creating fun and engaging gameplay. Today’s AI tools are still in the early stages of development and require significant human involvement to produce high-quality assets and content. We should evaluate AI based on its current strengths and how it can help accelerate iteration, while eliminating the tedious and time-consuming tasks involved in creating game assets and content. A significant amount of time and effort is invested in asset variations, retopology, rigging, localization, QA, code assistance, design research, and concept creation. AI can significantly accelerate these processes. This is where we should focus our AI efforts in game development today, rather than trying to replace humans in the game creation process. AI will help reduce laborious tasks, improve productivity, and provide tools that lower the need for specialists. 🔷 The Computer Entertainment Supplier's Association (CESA) reports that a significant 51% of surveyed Japanese game companies are integrating artificial intelligence into their development processes. This finding, based on a preview of the 2025 CESA Video Game Industry Report, highlights a growing trend among key industry players, including major publishers like Capcom, Konami, and Square Enix. AI applications are diverse, primarily focused on generating visual assets and character images, but also extending to story and text creation, as well as programming support. A notable 32% of these companies are leveraging AI to develop their own proprietary game engines, signaling a strategic investment in advanced technological capabilities. This widespread adoption underscores the potential of AI to enhance efficiency and creative output in game development. While some companies, such as Square Enix and Level-5, have openly embraced AI, others like Nintendo are taking a more cautious, originality-focused approach. The insights from CESA's report mirror broader industry discussions, as evidenced by sentiments at Gamescom, where independent studios lauded AI as a crucial development tool. This data provides a clear indicator of AI's increasing role in shaping the future of global interactive entertainment. ###### Abstract.

[GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2) ([GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2)) has had a tremendous impact on game production and promises lasting transformations. In the last five years since [GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2)’s inception, several studies, typically via qualitative methods, have explored its impact on game production from different settings and demographic angles. However, these studies often contextualise and consolidate their findings weakly with related work, and a big picture view is still missing. Here, we aim to provide such a view of GenAI’s impact on game production in the form of a qualitative research synthesis via meta-ethnography. We followed PRISMA-S to systematically search the relevant literature from 2020-2025, including major HCI and games research databases. We then synthesised the 10 eligible studies, conducting reciprocal translation and line-of-argument synthesis guided by eMERGe, informed by CASP quality appraisal. We identified nine overarching themes, provide recommendations, and contextualise our insights in wider game production trends.

###### Keywords:

generative AI, game development, systematic review, qualitative research synthesis, qualitative research appraisal, meta-ethnography, large-language models, text-to-image generation

## 1. Introduction

[GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2) ([GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2)) has disrupted and is transforming creative workflows across most industries and forms of creative practice. Game development, traditionally an early adopter of new technologies, is no exception. Transformation through [GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2) has been identified as a major and lasting trend in this domain ([Kultima 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib29)). The rapid uptake of [GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2) in commercial game production has also been confirmed through publishing data. Recent reporting on _Steam_ submissions indicates that at least 7% of all games released on the platform now disclose some form of AI usage for content creation, up from only 1% the year before ([Lambe 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib30)). This however likely still under-represents the actual scale of adoption, since disclosure is inconsistent. Around 60% of disclosed implementations involve visual asset generation, demonstrating how art pipelines are a central entry point for GenAI in game production. Reflecting this trend, _Valve_ has updated its _Steam_ content survey to require disclosure of both pre-generated AI content (produced during development) and live-generated AI content (produced during gameplay), with additional guardrail requirements for the latter.

The adoption of [GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2) in game production calls for research not only to improve systems and interaction modalities, but also to shape a societally and economically sustainable future of human-AI co-creation ([Kantosalo and Takala 2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib25)) and support the advancement of games as diverse cultural artefacts. We deem qualitative research the prime vehicle to explore this complex and rapidly evolving phenomenon, and existing studies have, amongst others, investigated how [GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2) reshapes workflows, raises ethical questions, and transforms relations between developers, artists, and players. Crucially though, while scholars have dedicated studies to the adoption of [GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2) in game production at a rarely seen and still increasing level of intensity, these investigations are often _limited_ to specific types of e.g.target demographic and production setting, or only a narrow aspect of the overall phenomenon. In addition, the research landscape remains _fragmented_ – reflecting a broader pattern in qualitative research, namely the “one-off problem of failing to build upon prior work”([Drisko 2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib16)). While some qualitative studies (Sec.[3.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#S3.SS2 "3.2. Consolidation in primary, empirical studies of  in Games ‣ 3. Related Work ‣ Generative AI in Game Development: A Qualitative Research Synthesis")) notably relate to previous work more extensively, this is (naturally) done in the service of distinguishing and motivating their own research focus or contributions, rather than taking a more neutral perspective. This state of affairs makes it difficult for researchers, practitioners, and policymakers to develop not only an understanding of the bigger picture, but also of the strength of empirical support for smaller phenomena identified within. A _synthesis_ is needed to translate insights across studies, identify consistencies and contradictions, and highlight areas requiring further exploration – both in terms of the studies phenomena and the methodology used.

Against this backdrop, our aim was to systematically review and synthesise qualitative research on the adoption and impact of [GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2) in game production. Specifically, we seek to answer the following research questions (RQs):

1.   (1)
How do existing qualitative studies differ, e.g.in research questions, methodology, demographics and setting?

2.   (2)
In what ways do findings across studies converge, complement, or contradict one another?

3.   (3)
Which overarching insights are conveyed about the impact of [GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2) on game production practices and cultures?

4.   (4)
Which conceptual, empirical, or methodological gaps remain? How might these shape future research priorities?

We address these questions through a _meta-ethnography_ as the arguably most established, interpretive [QRS](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id3) ([QRS](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id3)) method (see Sec.[4](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#S4 "4. Methods ‣ Generative AI in Game Development: A Qualitative Research Synthesis") for further justification). [QRS](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id3) has been highlighted as a systematic and reasonably robust (if undertaken by experienced qualitative researchers) method ([Campbell et al. 2011](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib11), p.69), capable of identifying saturated as well as underexplored areas of research ([Campbell et al. 2011](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib11), p.120). To ensure methodological rigour, we follow the _eMERGe_ reporting guidelines ([France et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib19)) for meta-ethnography, documenting our search and screening processes via _PRISMA-S_([Rethlefsen et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib60)), and appraising primary study quality using the _[CASP](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id10) ([CASP](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id10))_([Long et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib33)). We focus on studies from 2020-2025 investigating the use of publicly available [GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2) in “offline” game production (see Sec.[5.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#S5.SS1 "5.1. Eligibility Criteria ‣ 5. Selection of Primary Studies ‣ Generative AI in Game Development: A Qualitative Research Synthesis") for further details on scope. By drawing together insights from primary research, this synthesis not only consolidates a scattered evidence base, but also generates new hypotheses about the generalisability of observed phenomena.

In doing so, the paper provides the first integrated evidence base on [GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2)’s impact on game production, offering _industry stakeholders_ a clearer picture of emerging practices to adopt or avoid while equipping _researchers_, _funders_ and _policymakers_ with grounded insights to guide future investigations, support decisions and governance.

## 2. Background

Generative systems date back to early computer art, e.g, ([Cohen and McCorduck 1991](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib12); [Sims 1991](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib64)). Today, [GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2) ([GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2)) refers mainly to machine learning systems, particularly Transformers ([Vaswani et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib68)) and Diffusion Models ([Ho et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib22)). [GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2) is reshaping game design and development, creating both opportunities and challenges across creative and technical processes ([Ratican and Hutson 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib59)). We outline the advancements of [GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2) relevant to work work, focusing on text, image, 3D and audio content.

The development of Large language models [LLM](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id6) has revolutionised natural language processing, enabling remarkable language proficiency, capable of generating highly realistic text responses, based on little or no prior examples ([Brown et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib8)). The introduction of GPT-1 in 2018 ([Radford et al. 2018](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib56)) demonstrated that good performance can be obtained in wide range of natural language tasks and paved the way for current state-of-the-art models.

[LLM](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id6) continue to evolve rapidly, shaping both game writing and technical workflows. GPT-3 and GPT-3.5 ([Brown et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib8)) popularised conversational interaction through _ChatGPT_, while GitHub _Copilot_ demonstrated how code generation could accelerate engine scripting and gameplay logic. Google’s latest _Gemini 2.5_ model adds advanced multimodal reasoning, allowing integration of text, image, and audio in design workflows ([Oppenlaender 2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib49); [Inie et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib24)). At the engine level, Unity _Muse_([Unity Technologies 2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib67)) (released in Unity 6) now embeds LLM-based assistance directly into editor workflows, enabling code completion, asset search, and interaction prototyping without leaving the development environment.

With advances in [LLM](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id6), [TTIG](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id8) ([TTIG](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id8)) systems emerged ([Brown et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib8)). Caption-conditioned models had already shown that text could guide image generation ([Mansimov et al. 2015](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib39)), and CLIP ([Radford et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib55)) further advanced the field by learning visual concepts from natural language. OpenAI’s first DALL·E (2021) ([OpenAI 2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib47); [Ramesh et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib58)) combined a Transformer ([Vaswani et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib68)) with CLIP ([Ramesh et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib57)), while DALL·E 2 ([OpenAI 2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib48)) replaced the Transformer with Diffusion ([Ho et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib22)), producing images that were both more realistic and faithful to prompts. These breakthroughs paved the way for _Midjourney_([Midjourney 2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib44)) and _Stable Diffusion_([AI 2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib2); [Rombach et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib61)), now widely used for creative work.

Extending AI from two- to three-dimensional content generation was a natural step as image quality improved. Text2Mesh ([Michel et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib43)) introduced text-driven color and geometry editing of meshes, while CLIP-Forge ([Sanghi et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib62)) proposed zero-shot text-to-3D generation using CLIP embeddings without paired data. Recent systems can now transform simple text descriptions into 3D models, e.g., [Dai et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib14) apply semantic AI to generate conceptual 3D forms. Tools such as _Alpha 3D_([Alpha3D nd](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib4)), _Luma AI_([Luma AI, Inc. nd](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib34)) and _Meshy.ai_([Meshy LLC nd](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib41)) create textured, game-ready assets from text or image prompts. _Promethean AI_ assists designers by automating environment assembly ([Begemann and Hutson 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib5)), while _Genie 3_ generates interactive 3D worlds from a single prompt with evolving dynamics ([Parker-Holder et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib52)). Similarly, Tencent’s _Hunyuan-Game model_([Li et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib32)) extends generation to entire asset sets, including characters, effects, and video snippets trained on billions of game-specific resources.

Generative audio systems are beginning to fill critical gaps in sound and voice production, areas that often constrain smaller studios due to cost. Tools such as _Soundraw_([Soundraw nd](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib65)) provide AI-assisted adaptive music composition, while _ElevenLabs_([ElevenLabs Inc. nd](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib17)) enables lifelike voice acting with controllable accents and emotions. Diffusion-based systems like _Producer.ai_([Producer.ai (2025) formerly Riffusion](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib54)) and research frameworks such as _Meta’s Audiocraft_([Meta AI 2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib42)) expand possibilities for procedural soundscapes. These developments hint at future workflows where background scores, diegetic sound effects, and even NPC voices can be prototyped without traditional recording pipelines – an attractive prospect but one that raises concerns about replacing skilled human roles ([Elgammal et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib18); [Wingström et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib70)).

## 3. Related Work

To the best of our knowledge, noone has systematically synthesised qualitative research on the impact of [GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2) on game development or developer experiences more broadly. We relate this synthesis to existing work with similar objectives, while omitting work from other domains. We first delineate our synthesis from neighbouring reviews of different nature, which allows us to further articulate differences in scope and methods. We then repeat this for the few primary studies captured by our synthesis that could and made the effort of connecting their findings with previous work, complimenting their scholarship but also further motivating this comprehensive synthesis.

### 3.1. Reviews on [GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2) in Games

[Sweetser 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib66) did a scoping review and reflexive thematic analysis to map early research (2022 to Spring 2024) on LLMs and video games across five application themes. While most reviewed papers are technical, some qualitative observations from the interaction of developers with [GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2) are included, making this work the most related to ours. Key differences remain in technical focus, methodology, and timeframe. We focus exclusively on qualitative studies of developer experiences (2020 - Summer 2025) and, through meta-ethnography, provide an arguably more systematic, deeper and conceptually richer comparison and synthesis of existing work, which preserves the interpretations of the primary literature. To afford this depth of analysis and cater to a more specific stakeholder group, we limit our scope to game development, excluding uses such as live dialogue generation at runtime.

Similar to [Sweetser 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib66), [Moon et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib45) combine qualitative, empirical and quantitative, technical work to assess the relevance and challenges of [GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2) in educational game design across the perspective of designers, learners, instructors, and researchers. The review and analysis methodology as well as exact timeframe of covered literature is left opaque, and the report does not connect claims directly to specific qualitative insights from the primary literature. We, in contrast, provide a systematic and grounded synthesis of exclusively qualitative studies on [GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2)’s impact on game production, narrowing our scope to game developers’ insights while widening it to different production contexts and game types, including the design of educational games or games in educational contexts.

Other reviews draw on technical literature even more substantially to identify opportunities and challenges in using specific [GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2) technologies – often research prototypes – for game development. Focusing specifically on [GPT](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id7) ([GPT](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id7)) models and technical venues, [Yang et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib72); [Yang et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib73) provide a scoping review of GPT applications to games from 2020 to 2024, organising the literature into the five categories [PCG](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id5) ([PCG](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id5)), mixed-initiative game design, mixed-initiative gameplay, playing games, and game user research. The reviews do not report a specific literature search and analysis standard. Other technical reviews are methodologically more broad, but narrow their focus on specific applications in the game development pipeline. Drawing on the PRISMA standard, [Wu et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib71) systematically review papers demonstrating and advocating the use of [GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2) for game character creation across concept, modelling, animation, and behaviour design, from 2019 until Autumn 2024. While their emphasis is on design-time support, [Maleki and Zhao 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib37) review methods to implement [PCG](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id5) primarily at runtime, with a focus on [LLM](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id6). Their review and analysis covers literature from 2019 to 2023 but does not mention a specific standard. citetribeiro2024imageGenAI employ PRISMA to systematically review applications of image generation models for image-based game asset production, with a focus on image quality metrics. With papers from 2016 to 2023, the review also covers techniques that are not associated with [GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2) in the popular sense (cf.Sec.[2](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#S2 "2. Background ‣ Generative AI in Game Development: A Qualitative Research Synthesis")).

In contrast to these reviews, we focus exclusively on _synthesising_ rich, _qualitative_ insights from studies with the explicit goal to document _game developers’ experience_ with [GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2). Like the technical reviews above, this data also covers opportunities and shortcomings of [GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2) applications but is grounded in _concrete, in-situ insights from actual game development_ rather than researcher proposals on prototype potentiality. In common with these reviews, the present work also seeks to identify gaps and opportunities in research. However, these concern _gaps in evidence and methodology_, not in technology or specific applications. We explicitly exclude work on non-public research prototypes, focusing on serviced systems available to the _public_ to support the transfer of insights. Moreover, we focus on [GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2) technologies more generally, rather than specific flavours, and on its impact on game development more generally and across contexts, rather than a specific aspect of the pipeline. Arguably most crucially though, we conduct a methodologically rigorous, purely qualitative research synthesis via meta-ethnography ([Noblit and Hare 1988](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib46); [Cahill et al. 2018](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib10)), following established standards across the steps of literature search ([Rethlefsen et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib60), PRISMA-S,), quality appraisal ([Long et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib33), CASP,) as well as analysis and synthesis ([France et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib19), eMERGe,), facilitating the emergence of new conceptual insights. Epistemologically speaking, while the existing reviews primarily aggregate first-order interpretations from researchers, we interpret researchers’ second-order constructs of their participants’ experiences into third-order constructs as part of our synthesis, using participants’ first-order interpretations to ground the analysis and synthesis (see Sec.[4](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#S4 "4. Methods ‣ Generative AI in Game Development: A Qualitative Research Synthesis") for a distinction between aggregative and interpretative synthesis as well as 1 st/2 nd/3 rd-order interpretations).

### 3.2. Consolidation in primary, empirical studies of [GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2) in Games

Across our corpus of primary studies, only six out of 10 relate their findings to existing empirical work within game development but the depth and scope of that integration vary. Early contributions such as [Grow and Khosmood 2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib21) or [Vimpari et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib69), published when little directly comparable research existed, naturally offer limited integration within games. However, even among later studies, substantive cross-reference to other empirical studies in game production remains rare - additionally motivating this work. The most notable exceptions are [Boucher et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib6), which situates its findings within debates on authorship and labour within and outside games, and [Alharthi 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib3), which primarily relate to empirical studies to link production practices with broader questions of creativity and industry adoption.

W.r.t.these contributions, we provide a more comprehensive and systematic re-integration of their individual findings with the larger and up-to-date body of qualitative research. Given the interpretative nature of meta-ethnography, the partial integrations in the primary literature can be used as contrast and complement to our synthesis.

## 4. Methods

This paper aims to draw a bigger picture from existing qualitative research on how [GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2) has been adopted, received, and integrated within game development. To this end, we conducted a _[QRS](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id3) ([QRS](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id3))_ alongside an appraisal of the underlying qualitative research. While common in medical research ([Cahill et al. 2018](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib10)), these methods are only now gaining attention within [HCI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id4) ([HCI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id4)) and games research. In this section, we consequently motivate and introduce the core methods of this study, complemented by details on their execution in later parts.

### 4.1. Qualitative Research Synthesis

[QRS](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id3) ([QRS](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id3)) encompasses methods for systematically combining the data or interpretive findings from multiple qualitative studies to generate new knowledge and theory ([Drisko 2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib16)), and a “weight of evidence”([Campbell et al. 2011](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib11), pp.119-220) about a phenomenon. [QRS](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id3) can be broadly categorised into two types: _aggregative methods_ typically take a realist/pragmatist epistemology to pool and describe the original data (e.g. interview quotes) of large amounts of primary studies. In contrast, _interpretive methods_ take an intepretivist / constructivist stance to synthesise the interpretive findings (e.g. codes developed on these quotes) from typically smaller amounts of primary studies ([Drisko 2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib16)).

We conducted an _interpretive_[QRS](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id3) because (i) it extends and/or elaborates, rather than only describes, prior conceptualisation and theory; (ii) access to comprehensive raw data is not given in most of the identified relevant primary studies (Sec.[8](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#S8 "8. Description of Included Studies ‣ Generative AI in Game Development: A Qualitative Research Synthesis")); (iii) enables critical appraisal of the strengths and weaknesses of the original research; and finally, because (iv) interpretive QRS can make contextual and human diversity features more apparent across studies ([Drisko 2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib16), , quoting Paterson, 2012). Along these lines, [Campbell et al. 2011](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib11) also note its empowering function in involving “methods for combining multiple voices to seek new interpretations, rather than dismissing single case studies as locally bound”. While most relevant to our second RQ, (i) – (iii) are pivotal to addressing our third and fourth RQs (Sec.[1](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#S1 "1. Introduction ‣ Generative AI in Game Development: A Qualitative Research Synthesis")).

Following common terminology in QRS ([Noblit and Hare 1988](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib46); [Britten et al. 2002](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib7), e.g.) we refer to the raw data in the primary literature as “1 st-order interpretations”, thus emphasising that e.g.interview statements also constitute an individual’s interpretation of their personal experience. “2 nd-order interpretations” are then author’s interpretations of this data through qualitative analysis, e.g.codes assigned to such interview quotes. These are affected by the theories, individual perspectives and questions of the respective research team. Finally, “3 rd-order interpretations” emerge from the synthesis approach by critically comparing these second-order interpretations. We extend this taxonomy slightly, as elaborated on in Sec.[7](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#S7 "7. Data Extraction ‣ Generative AI in Game Development: A Qualitative Research Synthesis").

One of the few examples of [QRS](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id3) is the work of [McKechnie-Martin et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib40), who synthesised studies of player motivation through our chosen flavour of [QRS](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id3), elaborated on next. Here, we extend its application to the study of design and production-side engagements with emerging AI technologies, and more emphasis on methodological rigour.

### 4.2. Meta-Ethnography

We conducted a meta-ethnography, the pioneering and most widely used interpretive [QRS](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id3) method ([Drisko 2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib16)). Developed by [Noblit and Hare 1988](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib46) for synthesising data from ethnography and since extended ([France et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib19)), it introduces seven key steps, echoing those in quantitative systematic reviews, that have been widely adopted in related interpretive [QRS](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id3) methods:

1.   (1)
Selecting meta-ethnography and getting started

2.   (2)
Deciding what is relevant

3.   (3)
Reading included studies

4.   (4)
Determining how studies are related

5.   (5)
Translating studies into one another

6.   (6)
Synthesising translations

7.   (7)
Expressing the synthesis

Meta-ethnography enables conceptual translation across diverse studies while preserving their contextual and epistemic integrity ([Drisko 2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib16)). We primarily rely on _reciprocal_ rather than refutational _translation_, which has been considered “at the heart of why meta-ethnography is an effective method of qualitative synthesis”([Campbell et al. 2011](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib11), p.121). It consists of systematically relating 2 nd-order interpretations to each other across studies while noting their similarities and differences ([Drisko 2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib16)). To determine the latter, the researcher may need to take into account not only the descriptions of 2 nd-order interpretations (if given) but also the underlying 1 st-order interpretations (raw data).

The _synthesis_ is an inductive, iterative and evolving process in which the researcher produces 3 rd-order interpretations as conceptual abstractions by (potentially) re-analysing, relating and extending the original study authors’ 2 nd-order interpretations, while carefully preserving their grounding in the 1 st-order interpretations. Despite being described as separate phases, synthesis can already start during translation – as was also the case here. The synthesis culminates in a _line-of-argument_ narrative (also called “line-of-argument synthesis”([Drisko 2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib16))) in which 2 nd-order interpretations from different primary studies are brought together in a line of argument structured by our new 3 rd-order interpretations. The result “says something about the whole [phenomenon] based on studies of the parts”([Campbell et al. 2011](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib11), p.64) and should – also due to its interpretive nature – be considered new material complementing the primary studies ([Campbell et al. 2011](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib11), p.121).

For precision and transparency, we report our meta-ethnography in accordance with the 19 criteria outlined in the eMERGe framework ([France et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib19)).

### 4.3. Qualitative Research Appraisal

Acknowledging the ongoing debate on the value of quality appraisal in qualitative synthesis ([Long et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib33); [Cahill et al. 2018](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib10); [Dixon-Woods et al. 2008](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib15)), our study incorporates a formal study quality assessment. Following [Majid and Vanstone 2018](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib36)’s ([Majid and Vanstone 2018](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib36)) decision tool, we selected the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme ([CASP](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id10)) Qualitative Checklist as the most suitable instrument for the methodologically diverse studies in our dataset. In particular, we chose [CASP](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id10) for (1) being the most common appraisal tool in [QRS](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id3) that is (2) agnostic w.r.t. specific fields, (3) short and (4) relatively easy to employ. More specifically, we use the updated and optimised version of the tool by [Long et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib33). As a side-effect, appraisal can also contribute as interpretive aid and encourage the closer and repeated reading of primary studies ([Campbell et al. 2011](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib11), p.122).

We use quality appraisal not to determine the inclusion or exclusion of studies, but to (1) establish a nuanced weighting for each study’s relative contribution to the final synthesis ([Long et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib33)) and to (2) critically reflect on methodology as a lens to pinpoint gaps in research – contributing to answering our fourth research question (Sec.[1](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#S1 "1. Introduction ‣ Generative AI in Game Development: A Qualitative Research Synthesis")). With this choice, we address the central challenge of reconciling a study’s conceptual contribution with its methodological rigour. It is for the same challenge that we decided not to adopt the popular taxonomy of ’Key Paper’, ’Satisfactory’, and ’Fatally Flawed’ ([Dixon-Woods et al. 2008](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib15)) : for one, we would not wish to use the latter category as it might appear antagonising and hinder our goal to encourage methodological rigour in a constructive fashion; moreover, such a mutually exclusive system is ill-fitting if a single paper exhibits qualities from multiple categories. For instance, [Campbell et al. 2011](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib11) found that a study’s methodological reporting quality (e.g. “fatally flawed”) was not always reflective of its conceptual richness (potentially a “key paper”); similarly, [Dixon-Woods et al. 2008](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib15) document how reviewers faced a dilemma when assessing studies they found to be highly relevant despite flaws in their research conduct. Therefore, our approach separates these two judgements. First, following the framework provided by [Long et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib33), each paper is assigned a quality rating of Low, Medium, or High. This allows us to understand how strong the empirical support is for the interpretations subjected to our analysis and helps identify areas where further research is needed. Second, complementing this, we will flag studies that function as “Key Papers” in a conceptual sense. We adopt the definition used by [Malpass et al. 2009](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib38) who characterise a key paper as one “that is conceptually rich and could potentially make an important contribution to the synthesis”. This two-pronged appraisal system ensures that we are not overlooking conceptual innovation whilst still maintaining a clear view of the methodological rigour underpinning our synthesis.

## 5. Selection of Primary Studies

The process of searching and screening literature for a qualitative synthesis is acknowledged to be a challenging and multi-faceted phase ([Cahill et al. 2018](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib10)). To foster transparency and reproducibility, we implement the [PRISMA-S](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id11) ([PRISMA-S](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id11)) guidelines for reporting literature searches in systematic reviews ([Rethlefsen et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib60)). While the [eMERGe](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id9) ([eMERGe](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id9)) framework ([France et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib19)) provides guidance on meta-ethnography as a whole, we leverage [PRISMA-S](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id11) to add detail to the identification of relevant literature specifically (steps 5–7 in [eMERGe](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id9)). The PRISMA process is summarised in Fig.[1](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#S5.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 5.3. Selection Process ‣ 5. Selection of Primary Studies ‣ Generative AI in Game Development: A Qualitative Research Synthesis").

### 5.1. Eligibility Criteria

#### Inclusion

Our eligibility criteria (Tbl.[1](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#acmlabel1 "Table 1 ‣ Inclusion ‣ 5.1. Eligibility Criteria ‣ 5. Selection of Primary Studies ‣ Generative AI in Game Development: A Qualitative Research Synthesis")) were developed iteratively at the outset of the review and used to guide both the design of the search and the subsequent literature screening. We included studies that report _original empirical research_ using _qualitative data collection and analysis_ methods to examine the use of _GenAI_ systems within _game development_ contexts. Mixed-methods studies were eligible if the qualitative component was substantial and clearly reported. Our aim throughout was to prioritise studies that offer insight into how GenAI is used in practice over speculative or theoretical perspectives. To ensure relevance to current practices and a match of what is currently dominantly discussed under the umbrella of “[GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2)”, only studies published in the _last five years_ (January 2020 - June 2025) were considered, corresponding to the period in which publicly accessible GenAI tools became widely available to our target demographics. Studies were considered if they reported on participants’ _direct experience of game development_, either in professional roles or through situated creative production such as game jams or hackathons. We deliberately chose this wider focus as it includes people outside game industry who may eventually join the industry or contribute to game production from outside.

#### Exclusion

We excluded work that relied on custom-built or non-public [GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2) systems, as the corresponding findings may not easily generalise. We moreover excluded work that focused solely on technical implementation without empirically studying the product’s impact on human experience or practice. We also excluded studies that gathered data from players, students, or other stakeholders if these were not acting in a development capacity.

#### Limits and restrictions

We chose to limit our synthesis to qualitative paper in acknowledgement that [GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2) is a relatively new and rapidly evolving phenomenon within the game development industry. Therefore, exploratory research that captures rich, contextual insights, as provided through qualitative inquiry, is essential. Qualitative methods offer depth of understanding about how [GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2) is integrated into practice, revealing nuances that may not be accessible through purely quantitative research. We explicitly acknowledge the value of the latter and highlight the opportunity to inform it through the qualitative insights and research gaps identified here.

### 5.2. Search Strategy

We conducted a systematic literature search across academic databases relevant to [HCI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id4) and games research, complemented with a more open search. We initially searched the ACM Digital Library and Scopus via Elsevier, as they index the major publication venues in [HCI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id4) and technical game research. These further conducted manual searches in the DiGRA and the Foundations of Digital Games (FDG) proceedings to account for relevant work that may not be well indexed elsewhere. This was complemented by searches through Google Scholar to identify preprints and peer-reviewed work published in other venues. Two additional measures taken to expand the identified corpus are described in Sec.[5.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#S5.SS3 "5.3. Selection Process ‣ 5. Selection of Primary Studies ‣ Generative AI in Game Development: A Qualitative Research Synthesis").

The search terms were developed iteratively, informed by prior literature and exploratory database queries. Terms were grouped into four primary blocks: (1) game development contexts, (2) generative AI systems and models, (3) qualitative research design, and (4) conceptual framings and interaction modalities. Searches were initially piloted in the bibliographic databases ACM Digital Library and Scopus. They were then extended to the conference proceedings archives of DiGRA and FDG, as well as Google Scholar. Boolean operators and wildcards were used to manage linguistic variation, and search strings were adapted to suit the syntax requirements of each platform. Full search strategies, including all query variants, are included as Supplementary Materials.

### 5.3. Selection Process

The search strategy yielded an initial 191 records from the ACM Digital Library and 48 from Scopus. For Google Scholar, the first 100 results from our concatenated query were sorted by relevance and selected for review. In total, 339 records were retrieved. Duplicate entries were manually identified and removed, resulting in 320 unique records. Screening and selection followed a consensus-based approach involving all authors, ensuring agreement on inclusion decisions at both abstract/title screening and full-text review stages. Although modest in scale relative to large systematic reviews, the corpus reflects the specificity of our eligibility criteria as encoded in the search query. Based on the review of titles and abstracts, we identified seven studies that clearly met the eligibility criteria. A further 17 were flagged as borderline, requiring more detailed evaluation through full-text close reading with a focus on methodology and findings. This closer inspection resulted in the inclusion of three additional papers, establishing a preliminary corpus of 10 studies.

To ensure our primary literature pool was as comprehensive as possible, two further steps were taken. First, we conducted backward citation searching, manually examining the bibliographies of the ten included articles for any relevant studies missed by the initial search. Second, we contacted the first and last authors of these publications to enquire about any in-press or forthcoming work that might meet our eligibility criteria. Neither of these measures led to the inclusion of further studies; while we had a constructive dialogue with authors, their research was either not within scope or still work-in-progress at the time of starting our analysis. Thus, our final corpus includes ten studies.

We encountered two additional challenges during extraction. Firstly, the authors of primary studies often interpret similar phenomena with varying conceptual depth (e.g. a single code or a theme with subcodes). Secondly, 2 nd-order interpretations are given at various levels of conciseness (e.g.a code vs. an interpretive paragraph) and scarcity, with some papers letting the 1 st-order interpretations of the study participants speak largely for themselves. To mitigate this, we employed a multi-pronged extraction strategy. To address the risk of readily extractable interpretations (e.g. a clear table of codes from a thematic analysis) biasing the extraction of scarcer or absent interpretations, we first engaged with studies where 2 nd-order interpretations were more scarce or less concise. To systematically handle conceptual depth differences between papers, we adopted a two-step approach to the extraction itself.

1.   (1)
An initial extraction of top-level 2 nd-order interpretations was conducted across all studies.

2.   (2)
We then returned to studies where an already identified 2 nd-order interpretation was elaborated into a recognisable hierarchy.(e.g. [Boucher et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib6) on ethical resistance among early-career practitioners) to extract their more granular sub-themes in explicit relation to the parent concept.

This was done in line with guidance on preserving the context and meaning of interpretations within and across studies as described by [France et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib19), by retaining the wording and framing of 2 nd-order interpretations as given in the primary papers, documenting their provenance, as well as preserving the hierarchical links between interpretations as initialy set out by the authors. Where primary papers offered extensive first-order data but minimal authorial interpretation, as in [Grow and Khosmood 2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib21), we conducted our own thematic analysis to generate what we term “2 nd-order interpretations augmented”, enabling descriptive accounts to be integrated without conceptual flattening and ensuring comparability across the evidence base. Extracted interpretations were subsequently reviewed collaboratively by the research team, occasionally leading to the refinement or merging of interpretations to enhance clarity and coherence prior to synthesis. We clearly highlight these new interpretation in the visual documentation of our reciprocal translation, also showing all extracted interpretations (Sec.[9](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#S9 "9. Translation ‣ Generative AI in Game Development: A Qualitative Research Synthesis")). We acknowledge that data extraction and reciprocal translation are not fully distinct processes, in that (dis-) similarities between interpretations already become apparent during the extraction. We engaged in memo-taking to preserve these insights for the systematic analysis to follow.

### 8.1. Group A: Learning

[Boucher et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib6) studied a US summer programme simulating commercial game development with small, diverse intern teams. Its industry-readiness focus fostered debates on authorship and ethics alongside tool use, framed by the authors as resistance—where scepticism toward [GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2) intertwined with questions of identity and ethics in emerging professional cultures. In a UK classroom, [French et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib20) examined early integration of [LLM](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id6) and [TTIG](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id8) tools into individual projects, shaped by institutional constraints and faculty expertise. Unlike the collaborative, industry-simulated setting of [Boucher et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib6), this study highlighted how students negotiated technical limitations, with expectations defined more by tool deficiencies than transformative potential. A comparable classroom approach is seen in [Majgaard 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib35), who studied Danish engineering students building serious games in small teams, where [GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2) was treated as an additional teammate whose output required constant verification. This framing embedded [GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2) into reflective discussion and iterative design rather than using it as a discrete resource. Shifting toward a production-oriented model, [Shields et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib63) documented a US project where students and academics enhanced an educational visual novel. Like [Boucher et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib6), the work simulated professional production but within academic constraints, with managing [GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2) assets proving as time-consuming as traditional art.

Together, these four studies show how educational settings offered diverse entry points into [GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2) for game production. [Boucher et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib6) and [Shields et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib63) both simulated professional practice, the former focusing on interns’ negotiations of ethics and identity, the latter on asset management within mixed-experience teams. [French et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib20) examined individual student work constrained by tool limits, while [Majgaard 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib35) studied group projects that treated verification as reflective practice. Across cases, project format, participant background, and technology shaped how [GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2) was used and which challenges or opportunities emerged.

### 8.2. Group B: Production

[Alharthi 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib3) conducted a mixed-methods study involving industry professionals from the MENA region, Europe, North America, and parts of Asia. A survey of 42 respondents provided an overview of common use cases, with ideation, asset creation, and programming cited as primary applications, with further detail being captured through interviews. These revealed both enthusiasm and concern from participants in terms of potential efficiency gains and erosion of creative authenticity when integrating [GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2) into established workflows. Where [Alharthi 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib3) mapped practices across multiple studios, [Begemann and Hutson 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib5) turned inward to their own ten-day development project. Acting as developers, the authors documented the integration of [TTIG](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id8) and 3D generation tools into a game development pipeline. Their case highlights a persistent gap between producing high-quality 2D concept art and generating usable 3D assets, emphasising the limitations of current tools when applied to full production. An even more time-constrained perspective is offered by [Grow and Khosmood 2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib21), who studied a ChatGPT-based game jam. In contrast to the pipeline described by [Begemann and Hutson 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib5), this context prioritised rapid prototyping and improvisation, allowing participants to explore unconventional uses of [GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2). However, post-event reflections revealed that while participants valued the speed of idea generation, some reported a reduced sense of authorship over AI-assisted games. [Lankes and Stockl 2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib31) explored similar uses of ChatGPT but situated their work in longer-term indie studio practice. Interviewing three Austrian experts after they completed design exercises, the study shows that while [GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2) supported initial ideation, the outputs were not readily transferable to production without extensive refinement. While [Lankes and Stockl 2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib31) focused on a small number of experts, [Panchanadikar and Freeman 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib51) scaled outward to examine more than 3000 posts from international online developer communities. Discussions often portrayed [GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2) as a co-worker that could accelerate solo workflows, particularly for non-specialist tasks, while also producing errors that required close supervision. Concerns were also raised about asset quality, copyright issues, as well as over-reliance on the technology. The study further captured how community norms shaped this discourse, with enthusiasm for innovation tempered by peer to peer caution. [Vimpari et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib69) offered yet another perspective through interviewing professionals from Finnish game studios, focusing on their use of [TTIG](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id8). Their study reveals both optimism about the creative potential of the technology as well as unease over ethical challenges and commercial pressures to adopt new tools. The authors note that these tensions were often framed in pragmatic terms, attempting to balane artistic ambitions with the realities of market competitiveness.

Pictured as a whole, these studies span a range of professionals settings, from cross-regional industry surveys to focused case studies, time-limited events, and large-scale analyses of community discourse. Together, they capture different facets of [GenAI](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#id2) use in professional game development, documenting both tool integration and the wider conversations that are shaping their adoption.

## 9. Translation

#### Procedure

Similarly to [Campbell et al. 2011](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib11), we applied reciprocal translation in two stages: first within, and then across the Learning and Production groups. Following Campbell, we adopted a chronological procedure with an “index” paper: we designated the oldest included study as the index against which other were compared ([Campbell et al. 2011](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib11), p. 47, 65), then proceeded in publication order, adding one paper at a time and updating the synthesis at each step ([Campbell et al. 2011](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#bib.bib11), p.57). All extracted 2 nd-order interpretations were imported into ATLAS.ti 25 as discrete nodes, linking to their source study. In this context, we use “scope” to denote the level or focus of a claim (e.g. whether a finding refers to asset inclusion, pipeline efficiency, or adoption attitudes); in the rest of the paper, all references to “scope” follow this analytic meaning. Within each evidence set, interpretations were related using a custom vocabulary of semantic connectors:

Translates: 
Conceptually equivalent at the same scope.

Supports: 
Adds further first-order interpretations of the same type.

Enriches: 
Introduces a new dimension to an existing concept.

Contradicts: 
Opposes another interpretation at the same scope.

Originally part of: 
Retains an author-defined interpretive hierarchy from the primary source.

All but the last relationship connect nodes from different primary studies. The last enables us to distinguish original hierarchies from those developed through the synthesis process for maximum transparency. Relations were initially assigned by a member of the research team and then validated collaboratively until consensus was reached. Cases of uncertainty or disagreement were discussed in group review sessions.

Once each group’s network was internally connected, the two networks were brought together into a shared workspace. Cross-group translation then proceeded by identifying additional _Translates_, _Supports_, _Enriches_ and _Contradicts_ between interpretations originating in different environments. This stage was iterative: where relation scope was ambiguous, we returned to the primary texts to verify the interpretation in context. The final integrated network retained all relation types, with group-specific and cross-group structures to remaining visible for subsequent synthesis.

#### Outcome

Relating the studies yielded a dense _Production_ network (79 unique interpretations, 105 links) and a more compact _Learning_ network (37 unique interpretations, 35 links), plus a layer crossing both settings (24 links). In the rest of this article and accompanying figures we colour-code each of these primary groups in shades of _green_ and _purple_, respectively, to easily distinguish contributions from each group. Across all three spaces, most relations either _Enrich_ or _Support_ an existing interpretation rather than asserting strict equivalence. In _Production_ over half of the links (54%) _enrich_ the linked interpretation with new conditions or mechanisms, while 18% connect further 1 st-order interpretations _supporting_ the same claim. Only 12% are _Translates_ relations and _Contradicts_ are very rare (1.9%), indicating that studies more often build upon rather than accurately duplicating or opposing one another. In _Learning_, the pattern shifts slightly towards corroboration, with _Supports_ (49%) roughly matching _Enriches_ (43%) and a similar scarcity of _Translates_ and _Contradicts_.

Cross-environment links are dominated by _Enriches_ (83%), with very few _Translates_ and _Contradicts_. This pattern reflects that when _Learning_ and _Production_ connect, they add contextual detail rather than asserting full equivalence across domains. Where contradictions occur, they often mark boundaries in framing or scope, as in _“LS23 - GAI as colleague”_ contradicting _“BC23 - AI as Tool”_, reflecting differences in role conceptualisation between classroom and industry contexts. This relational map was the basis for our translation, producing a connected network of related interpretations which made visible discrete translation groupings. Each node retained the verbatim 2 nd-order interpretation from its source, linked to the underlying 1 st-order data, enabling direct traceability. Figure [2](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.11898v1#S9.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Outcome ‣ 9. Translation ‣ Generative AI in Game Development: A Qualitative Research Synthesis") shows a close-up of the “ideation support” translation cluster, illustrating how this pattern plays out in practice. Links to _“AH25 - Prototyping and Efficiency”_ and _“VG23 - Systems strenghts & weaknesses - inspiration”_ enrich the core idea by adding mechanisms and context-specific detailing, whilst links such as _“MJ24 - Brainstorm”_ support the claim by providing concrete examples from the classroom.
